Count
kownt
v.t. (to number; also to reckon or account something to be so; rendering Hebrew chashab, manah, Greek logizomai, hegeomai)
From Old French conter, Latin computare, to reckon. The two English senses — to enumerate and to consider — are both in Scripture, and the second carries the doctrine of imputation.

Biblical Definition

To count is both to enumerate and to reckon a thing to be so, and the second sense is theologically decisive. It is the word behind imputation: Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness (Romans 4:3), where the Greek logizomai is a bookkeeping term — something is entered to an account that was not there before. Paul then applies the same verb to his own ledger, counting his considerable religious assets as loss for Christ. In the plainer sense, the Lord Jesus makes counting a duty of discipleship: “which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?” (Luke 14:28) — a warning against following Him on an unexamined impulse, delivered to great multitudes rather than to hesitant enquirers. James commands a reckoning that runs against the grain of the senses: “count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations” (James 1:2), which is not the pretence that trials are pleasant but the deliberate entry of them on the right side of the ledger, on the stated ground that trying works patience. Moses asks for the arithmetic that produces wisdom: “So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom” (Psalm 90:12). And Balaam, of all people, wishes for an end he will not have: “Who can count the dust of Jacob…? Let me die the death of the righteous” (Numbers 23:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

To number, and to reckon a thing to be so. The second sense carries imputation. Christ requires counting the cost before following; James commands counting trials as joy; Moses asks to number his days; Balaam wishes for a righteous man's death.

expand to see more

COUNT, v.t. [Fr. compter; L. computo; con and puto, to throw together.] To number; to tell or name one by one, for ascertaining the whole number of units in a collection.

2. To reckon; to preserve a reckoning; to compute.

3. To esteem; to account; to reckon; to think, judge, or consider. I count them but dung. Phil. 3.

4. To impute; to charge. It was counted to him for righteousness. Rom. 4.

COUNT, n. Reckoning; the act of numbering; as, this is the number according to my count.

Key Scripture

Luke 14:28 — "For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?"

James 1:2 — "My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations;"

Psalm 90:12 — "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom."

Numbers 23:10 — "Who can count the dust of Jacob, and the number of the fourth part of Israel? Let me die the death of the righteous, and let my last end be like his!"

Modern Corruption

“Count the cost” has been detached from the discipleship it introduces and turned into generic prudential advice — while James 1:2 is preached as a demand for cheerfulness in suffering that the verse does not make.

expand to see more

Luke 14:28 is quoted in stewardship seminars and business talks as counsel about planning, and the parable does teach that. But the Lord Jesus tells it in the middle of the most severe passage on discipleship in the Gospels: whoever does not hate father and mother and his own life also cannot be His disciple; whoever bears not his cross cannot be His disciple; and the paragraph closes, so likewise, whosoever he be of you that forsaketh not all that he hath, he cannot be my disciple (Luke 14:33). The tower and the king going to war are illustrations of that, and they are addressed to great multitudes who were following Him easily. He is thinning a crowd on purpose. Preaching that reduces the passage to prudence has performed the opposite operation from the one the passage exists to perform.

James 1:2 suffers a different distortion, and it wounds people. Preached as a command to feel joy in affliction, it makes a grieving Christian guilty for grieving, and it flatly contradicts the Bible's own record — the Psalms of lament, the Lord weeping at Lazarus's tomb, Paul's sorrow upon sorrow at Epaphroditus's illness. Count is hegeomai, to reckon, to judge a thing to be the case. James is commanding a verdict, not a feeling: the trial is producing patience, patience is producing completeness, and the believer is to enter it on the ledger accordingly while it still hurts. That is a demand on the mind, made available to the man who is weeping, and it is far more useful to him than an instruction to stop.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chashab (to reckon, impute, account) and manah (to number, apportion); Greek logizomai (to reckon, the imputation word), hegeomai (to consider, deem), and psephizo (to count with pebbles, the verb in Luke 14:28).

expand to see more

Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to reckon, impute, account; the verb in Genesis 15:6, counted it to him for righteousness.

Hebrew manah (H4487) — to number, count out, appoint; used of numbering days and of God appointing the great fish.

Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, credit to an account; the technical term of imputation in Romans 4.

Greek hegeomai (G2233) — to lead, consider, deem; the verb in James 1:2 and Philippians 3:7-8.

Greek psephizo (G5585) — to count with pebbles, calculate; the verb in Luke 14:28 and Revelation 13:18.

Usage

"“Counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish” — told to great multitudes, to thin them."

"“Count it all joy” — a verdict commanded of the mind, not a feeling demanded of the heart."

"“Teach us to number our days” — the arithmetic that produces wisdom."
